## Code

```{r}
library(httr2) 
library(tidyverse)

api_key <- Sys.getenv("GOVINFO_API_KEY")

body <- list(query = 'collection:(CHRG) AND "Committee on Foreign Relations"', pageSize = 100, offsetMark = "*", sorts = list(list(field = "publishdate", sortOrder = "DESC")))

found <- request("https://api.govinfo.gov/search") |>
req_url_query(api_key = Sys.getenv("GOVINFO_API_KEY")) |>
req_body_json(body) |>
req_perform() |>
resp_body_json()
```

```{r}
data_1to10 <- found$results[1:10]
data_1to10[[1]]

package_ids <- sapply(data_1to10, function(x) x$packageId)
titles <- sapply(data_1to10, function(x) x$title)
date <- sapply(data_1to10, function(x) x$dateIssued)

data <- data.frame(package_id = package_ids, date = date, title = titles)
data 
```

```{r}

dir.create("govinfo_downloads", showWarnings = FALSE)

for (i in 1:10) {

  pdf_url <- data_1to10[[i]]$download$pdfLink
  package_id <- data_1to10[[i]]$packageId

  request(pdf_url) |>
    req_url_query(api_key = api_key) |>
    req_perform(path = paste0("govinfo_downloads/", package_id, ".pdf"))}

data_1to10
list.files("govinfo_downloads") 
```

```{r}
download_log <- data.frame(
  package_id = sapply(data_1to10, function(x) x$packageId),
  date = sapply(data_1to10, function(x) x$dateIssued),
  title = sapply(data_1to10, function(x) x$title),
  file = paste0("govinfo_downloads/", sapply(data_1to10, function(x) x$packageId), ".pdf"))

download_log

write.csv(download_log, "govinfo_download_log.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r}
manual <- read.csv("govinfo-search-results.csv")
names(manual) 

manual_10 <- manual |>
  arrange(desc(publishdate)) |>
  slice_head(n = 10)

setdiff(package_ids, manual_10$packageId)
setdiff(manual_10$packageId, package_ids) 
```

## Comparison

Initially, the manual search and API search produced different results
because the GovInfo website sorted results by relevance, while the API
sorted them by publication date in descending order. After changing the
manual search to "Newest First," both methods returned the same ten
hearings.

## Reports

### 1. Usability of Downloaded Documents

The GovInfo API provided access to congressional hearing documents and
their associated metadata. I successfully retrieved the ten most recent
Senate Foreign Relations Committee hearings and downloaded their PDF
files.

Although PDFs are useful for reading and preserving the original
documents, they are less convenient for quantitative or text analysis.
To convert these ten PDFs into a structured dataset, I had to extract
relevant information, such as hearing titles and dates and organize it
into a table. For text analysis, it was inconvenient to extract the text
from each document, clean formatting inconsistencies, and combine the
documents into a corpus.

### 2. Difficulties and Improvements

One difficulty was handling the nested JSON structure returned by the
API. Some fields, such as governmentAuthor and download, contained
multiple values, which caused errors when I attempted to convert the
entire response into a data frame. I resolved this issue by extracting
only the variables needed for the assignment.

Another issue occurred when comparing the API results with the manually
exported CSV file. Initially, the two methods returned different
hearings because the GovInfo website sorted results by relevance, while
the API sorted them by publication date in descending order. After
changing the manual search to "Newest First," both methods returned the
same ten hearings.

The data collection process could be improved by using alternative
formats, such as TXT/HTML or XML, rather than relying exclusively on
PDFs. These formats may make text extraction and automated processing
easier. In addition, the API provides metadata, including document
titles, identifiers, dates, and download links, which can be organized
into a dataset without opening each document.

### 3. Advantages of Using an API

Compared with the GovInfo search page, the API allows users to automate
searches, specify sorting criteria, retrieve structured metadata, and
download multiple documents programmatically. Compared with last week's
web scraping, the API provides a more direct and standardized way to
access data without relying on the structure of a website's HTML.
